query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multiphase eutectic high‐entropy alloys, simultaneous exposure to sliding wear and corrosion at elevated temperature accelerates degradation because mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective oxide films at phase boundaries, exposing dissimilar phases that form localized galvanic cells. These galvanic interactions preferentially attack the less noble phase, further undermining the oxide protection and amplifying both wear and corrosion in a positive feedback loop.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high‐entropy alloy characterized by a ductile matrix and discrete intermetallic or second phases arranged in a eutectic microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures under controlled sliding wear conditions in a corrosive medium (for example, a chloride-containing solution) mimicking aggressive service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries between dissimilar microstructural constituents which foster localized galvanic coupling.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear erodes the initially protective oxide films at the phase interfaces, thereby exposing fresh surfaces with differing electrochemical potentials. The resulting potential differences set up localized galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion of the less noble phase, which in turn further destabilizes oxide protection and enhances subsequent wear in a synergistic manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a homogeneous single‐phase baseline or tests where wear and corrosion occur individually, the multiphase eutectic alloy will exhibit a noticeably higher overall degradation rate. Both individual wear (evidenced by increased material loss) and localized corrosion (shown by higher corrosion current density and pit formation at phase boundaries) are expected to be amplified.
generation.baseline: A comparable single‐phase high‐entropy alloy or tests conducted under isolated wear or corrosion conditions at lower temperatures where passive film integrity is maintained.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to operate under conditions of elevated temperature with active sliding wear in corrosive media; variations outside these parameters (such as lower temperatures or static conditions) may not exhibit the same synergistic effects.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative acceleration of degradation is supported by the proposed galvanic mechanism, the exact quantitative enhancement of wear and corrosion rates under combined exposure requires further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with a multiphase eutectic high‐entropy alloy exhibiting distinct phase boundaries and a baseline set with a homogeneous single-phase microstructure. Subject both sets to identical testing conditions involving simultaneous sliding wear and exposure to a corrosive chloride environment at an elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C) for a predetermined time.
measurements: Total mass loss (to quantify overall degradation)
Wear track profiling (depth and morphology via microscopy)
Electrochemical corrosion measurements (such as corrosion current density using potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface characterization (SEM/EDS analysis at phase boundaries for signs of localized galvanic corrosion)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase alloy does not show a statistically significant synergistic increase in both wear and corrosion—i.e., if its total degradation is not greater than the sum of the individual degradation modes observed in the homogeneous baseline—then the hypothesis that inter-phase galvanic coupling due to wear-induced oxide film removal drives the accelerated degradation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. drafts.hypothesis: Mechanical wear continuously removes the passivating oxide film on the eutectic high-entropy alloy, exposing dissimilar micro-phases that form local galvanic couples. This micro-galvanic effect, in the presence of elevated temperature, accelerates both wear and corrosion beyond their individual rates.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with an established passive oxide film at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperature.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperature sufficient to enhance chemical kinetics, a chemically aggressive medium, and a wear regime that periodically removes the passive film.
drafts.structural_mediator: Microstructural heterogeneity at the eutectic interfaces, which promotes galvanic interactions between phases after oxide removal.
drafts.mechanism: The mechanical wear erodes the protective oxide film and exposes underlying micro-phases with different electrochemical potentials. This difference establishes local galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion. The combined effect of mechanical disruption and localized corrosion leads to a feedback loop, which further expedites material degradation under elevated thermal conditions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (non-worn or non-corroded conditions), the total degradation will increase. Individually, the wear response will show increased material removal due to a loss of oxide protection, and the corrosion response will show enhanced localized attack at phase boundaries. The synergy of these effects is predicted to yield an accelerated net degradation rate compared with the sum of individual wear and corrosion effects observed in isolation.
drafts.baseline: The alloy under conditions where wear and corrosion occur separately or at lower temperatures where the protective film is stable.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the elevated temperature undermines the stability of the passive film, the applied wear is sufficient to mechanically remove the oxide layer, and the microstructure exhibits sufficient electrochemical potential differences between phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. For one set, maintain the passive oxide film by applying a protective coating before subjecting the sample to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature. The control set remains uncoated. Measure wear rates, corrosion depths, and overall degradation over identical time intervals.
measurements: Quantitative mass loss due to wear
Corrosion pit depth and density (via microscopy)
Electrochemical potential mapping at microstructural scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated (film-preserved) samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in combined degradation (both wear and corrosion rates) compared to the uncoated samples, then the hypothesis that wear-induced oxide removal and subsequent micro-galvanic corrosion accelerate the degradation is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Accelerated coupled degradation in the multi‐phase eutectic HEA arises from differential oxidation at phase boundaries, leading to local galvanic cells. In this scenario, wear mechanically removes protective oxides preferentially from the less oxidation‐resistant phase, exposing fresh material that rapidly oxidizes. The interface between phases then acts as a conduit for galvanic coupling, which amplifies both the corrosion and wear processes when the alloy is exposed simultaneously to mechanical stress and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature.
drafts.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct phases that are spatially organized and well-bonded, each possessing differing oxidation stabilities.
drafts.intervention: Exposing the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear and a corrosive environment (e.g., saline or similar electrolyte) at elevated temperature conditions.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperature (consistent with service conditions), controlled mechanical wear (identical load and sliding speed), and a defined corrosive medium; compared to baselines with isolated wear or isolated corrosion under the same thermal conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries within the eutectic microstructure, which facilitate differential oxidation and thereby promote localized galvanic coupling between the more and less oxidation-resistant phases.
drafts.mechanism: Wear removes protective oxide scales more efficiently from the phases that oxidize rapidly. This leads to intermittent exposure and subsequent rapid oxidation. At the phase interfaces, the difference in oxidation and electrochemical potentials creates galvanic cells, accelerating the corrosion process. The resulting localized corrosion further weakens the material, enhancing wear, and thus creating a positive feedback loop that drives accelerated total degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline where only wear or only corrosion is applied, the sample under simultaneous exposure will exhibit a significantly higher total degradation. Specifically, both individual wear and corrosion rates will be enhanced beyond a simple additive effect due to the synergy from localized galvanic action at phase boundaries.
drafts.baseline: A matched sample set tested under conditions of isolated wear and isolated corrosion at the same elevated temperature, where each degradation mode operates without the synergistic effect of the other.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is relevant under conditions where the alloy's multiphase structure is intact, the wear is sufficient to remove protective oxides but not to completely obliterate the microstructure, and the temperature is high enough to promote rapid oxidation without causing phase transformations. It assumes no external inhibitors that would otherwise stabilize the protective oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion at an elevated temperature, and a control set exposed individually to wear and corrosion under identical temperature conditions. Use identical alloy batches with the documented eutectic microstructure. Quantify mass loss, wear track depth, and corrosion rates. Additionally, perform microstructural and surface chemistry analyses focused on the phase boundaries to detect signs of localized galvanic corrosion.
measurements: Wear track profiling (e.g., depth and width measurements)
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (e.g., corrosion potentials and current densities)
Microscopic analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS) along phase boundaries to observe oxide formation and degradation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimen subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion does not exhibit a statistically significant synergistic increase in total degradation (i.e., the combined effect is not greater than the sum of the isolated effects) and phase boundary analyses do not reveal evidence of localized galvanic corrosion relative to the baseline, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys, the simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature are accelerated by galvanic interactions between the distinct phases. Specifically, the potential differences between a relatively noble ductile FCC matrix and the adjacent intermetallic (e.g., σ or Laves) phases create localized galvanic cells. When these galvanic couples operate under high temperature, the increased oxidation and diffusion kinetics rapidly disrupt the integrity of any passive films. The combined effect of preferential attack on the less noble phase and the mechanical removal (or rupture) of the protective oxide layer during wear leads to a synergistic acceleration of overall degradation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy having a dual microstructure composed of a ductile FCC matrix and discrete intermetallic (σ/Laves) phases
drafts.intervention: Simultaneous exposure to sliding wear and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., ≥600 °C) in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) while undergoing friction (pin-on-disc or reciprocating wear tests)
drafts.structural_mediator: The galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries between the FCC matrix and intermetallic precipitates
drafts.mechanism: Under elevated temperature, the potential difference between the phases drives localized galvanic corrosion, selectively attacking the less noble intermetallic phase. This localized corrosion undermines the continuity of the passivating oxide layer that normally protects the surface. When mechanical wear occurs simultaneously, the weakened oxide film is more readily removed or ruptured, exposing fresh material to further corrosion. The cycle of passive film degradation and abrasive removal accelerates total material loss.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy without pronounced phase contrast (or tested under lower temperature), the multiphase eutectic HEA will show an increased overall degradation rate. Individually, the corrosion response (e.g., higher corrosion current density) and the wear response (e.g., higher wear volume loss) are both predicted to be amplified. Their combined, synergistic action is expected to produce a total degradation response significantly higher than the sum of the separate effects.
drafts.baseline: A matched high‐entropy alloy with a more homogeneous (single-phase) microstructure or tests conducted at lower temperatures where diffusion and oxidation kinetics are reduced
drafts.boundary: Tests must be performed at elevated temperature (e.g., ≥600 °C) under simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., via pin-on-disc or reciprocating sliding tests) and in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution); variations outside these conditions may not reveal the same synergistic effects

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one consisting of the multiphase eutectic HEA exhibiting distinct FCC and intermetallic phases, and another with a similar overall composition but processed (e.g., via post-heat treatment or alternative processing) to yield a predominantly single-phase, homogeneous microstructure. Expose both sample sets to identical testing conditions with simultaneous sliding wear and immersion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at an elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C) for a fixed period.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N·m) using standardized pin-on-disc or reciprocating wear tests
Electrochemical corrosion rate (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current density)
Surface and cross-sectional characterization of passive film integrity (using SEM/EDS) post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase eutectic alloy does not exhibit significantly higher combined degradation (i.e., both higher wear and corrosion rates, and more disrupted passive films) compared to the homogeneous single-phase baseline under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that inter-phase galvanic coupling is responsible for the accelerated coupled degradation would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is driven by micro‐galvanic coupling between the dissimilar phases. In this scenario, a protective oxide film forms differently on the ductile matrix (e.g., FCC) and the hard second phase (e.g., σ phase), and under mechanical wear, the fragile oxide at the phase interfaces repeatedly spalls off. This exposes fresh, compositionally disparate surfaces that accelerate localized galvanic corrosion and, in turn, intensify wear by producing abrasive particles.
drafts.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic HEA having a microstructure with a ductile FCC matrix and a hard, brittle second phase (e.g., σ phase) arranged in a eutectic/hypereutectic morphology, with an inherent tendency to form a nonuniform protective oxide layer at high temperature.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and a chloride-rich corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 600 °C).
drafts.conditions: The tests are conducted under controlled sliding wear conditions (with specified load and speed), in a corrosive electrolyte at elevated temperature where oxide formation occurs, to mimic service conditions that induce both mechanical and chemical degradation.
drafts.structural_mediator: The interfaces between the two distinct phases act as micro‐galvanic sites where differential oxide formation and breakdown occur, mediating localized electrochemical potential differences.
drafts.mechanism: Due to phase-dependent oxidation, the protective oxide film is nonuniform and mechanically brittle. Under the imposed wear conditions, the oxide repeatedly spalls, exposing fresh substrate areas with different electrochemical potentials that promote local galvanic corrosion. The recurring cycle of oxide reformation and removal leads to a synergistic escalation of both wear and corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a homogeneous single-phase HEA baseline, the multi-phase eutectic alloy is expected to display a notably higher overall degradation rate. Specifically, the multi-phase alloy should show increased mass loss from wear (due to repetitive oxide spallation and abrasive particle formation) and higher localized corrosion rates (from enhanced galvanic interactions) at elevated temperatures.
drafts.baseline: A comparable HEA with a homogeneous (single-phase) microstructure that forms a more uniform oxide film, tested under the same elevated temperature, wear, and corrosive conditions.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to operate under high-temperature conditions in corrosive (chloride-containing) environments when active sliding wear is present. At lower temperatures, in non-corrosive or static conditions, the coupling effect between wear and corrosion may be negligible.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys with nearly identical bulk compositions: one with a multi-phase eutectic microstructure (containing both FCC and σ phases) and one with a homogeneous, single-phase structure. Subject both samples to identical tests combining sliding wear and immersion in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at an elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C) over a fixed period. Monitor the surface evolution over time using microscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and mass loss measurements.
measurements: Wear scar dimensions and morphology (to assess abrasive damage)
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion current density, impedance spectra)
Surface imaging (to document oxide film continuity and spallation events)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase eutectic HEA does not exhibit significantly higher wear-induced mass loss and accelerated corrosion (as indicated by more pronounced discontinuous oxide layers and greater localized corrosion pits) than the homogeneous alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that the micro-galvanic mechanism driven by differential oxide film behavior is responsible for the accelerated degradation is falsified.
